all-purpose thread.d: Medium-weight polyester thread that works for most sewing. Use the same thread on top and in the bobbin.

backstitch.d: By machine: a few stitches sewn in reverse at the start and end of a seam to lock it. By hand: a strong stitch where each stitch goes back to meet the last one.

baste.d: To sew long, temporary stitches that hold pieces in place until the real seam is sewn. Basting is easy to pull out.

bias.d: The 45° diagonal across woven fabric. It stretches much more than the grain, which is why bias-cut garments drape and bias strips bend around curves.

bobbin.d: The small spool of thread that sits under the needle plate. Its thread locks with the top thread to form each stitch.

boxed corner.d: A corner flattened into a triangle and stitched straight across, giving a bag or pouch a flat bottom.

canvas.d: A sturdy, tightly woven cotton fabric used for bags, aprons, and outerwear. Duck is a similar, smoother fabric.

casing.d: A folded and stitched tunnel that holds elastic or a drawstring.

clip.d: A small straight snip into a seam allowance, stopping just short of the stitching. Clips let inward curves and corners lie flat.

collar.d: The piece that finishes and frames the neckline. On a shirt, it folds over a band called the collar stand.

crosswise grain.d: The direction from one selvedge to the other, across the fabric. It has a little more give than the lengthwise grain.

cuff.d: A band that finishes the end of a sleeve or pant leg.

edgestitch.d: A line of stitching very close to an edge or fold, usually about 1/8 in away. It holds layers flat and looks crisp.

feed dogs.d: The little metal teeth under the presser foot that move the fabric along as you sew.

fray.d: When threads unravel from a cut edge of woven fabric. Finishing the edges stops it.

grain.d: The direction the threads run in a woven fabric. Lengthwise grain runs parallel to the selvedge; crosswise grain runs across.

grainline.d: The long arrow on a pattern piece. Lay it parallel to the selvedge so the piece is cut on grain.

handwheel.d: The wheel on the right side of the machine that moves the needle by hand. Always turn the top of it toward you.

hem.d: The finished bottom edge of a garment or item, usually folded up and stitched.

knit.d: Fabric made of rows of interlocking loops, like a t-shirt or sweater. Knits stretch.

ladder stitch.d: A hand stitch that closes a gap between two folded edges. The stitches cross straight between the folds and disappear when pulled tight.

lengthwise grain.d: The direction parallel to the selvedge. It's the strongest direction and barely stretches. Most pattern pieces follow it.

lining.d: A second layer inside a bag or garment that hides the seams and raw edges and makes it feel nicer.

needle plate.d: The metal plate under the presser foot, with a hole for the needle and guide lines for seam allowances.

needle size.d: Machine needles are sized with two numbers, like 80/12. The bigger the number, the thicker the needle.

notch a curve.d: Cutting little V shapes out of the seam allowance on an outward curve, so it lies flat when turned. (On patterns, a notch is also a small mark used to match pieces: you'll meet that in level 4.)

pinking shears.d: Scissors with zigzag blades. The zigzag edge frays less than a straight cut.

pivot.d: Turning the fabric around the needle (needle down, foot up) to sew a sharp corner.

placket.d: A finished opening in a garment, like the doubled strip that holds the buttons on a shirt front.

press.d: Lifting the iron, setting it down, and holding it, instead of sliding it. Pressing shapes and flattens without stretching.

press open.d: Spreading the two seam allowances apart and pressing them flat on either side of the seam.

presser foot.d: The metal foot that holds the fabric flat against the feed dogs while you sew. Lower it before every seam.

pressing cloth.d: A piece of plain cotton or organza laid between the iron and your fabric to prevent shine and scorching.

prewash.d: Washing and drying fabric before cutting, the same way you'll wash the finished item, so it shrinks before you sew it.

quilting cotton.d: A medium-weight, plain-woven cotton. Stable, easy to sew and press: the best fabric to learn on.

raw edge.d: A cut edge of fabric that isn't finished yet, so it can fray.

right side.d: The front of the fabric, meant to show on the outside. In Notch diagrams it's colored with dots.

right sides together.d: Placing two pieces face to face, pretty sides touching, before sewing. The seam ends up on the inside.

rotary cutter.d: A round blade on a handle, rolled along a ruler on a cutting mat. Great for straight cuts.

running stitch.d: The simplest hand stitch: in and out along a line. Used for basting and gathering.

seam.d: The line of stitching that joins two pieces of fabric.

seam allowance.d: The distance between the cut edge and the stitching line. Notch always uses 5/8 in (1.5 cm), like most store patterns.

seam gauge.d: A short ruler with a sliding marker, for measuring and repeating small distances like hems.

seam ripper.d: A small tool with a sharp hook for cutting and removing stitches.

selvedge.d: The tightly woven, finished edge along both long sides of fabric. It doesn't fray.

serger.d: A machine that sews a seam, trims the edge, and wraps it in thread all at once. Nice to have, never required.

shank.d: The short stem under a button, made of wrapped thread or built into the button. It gives the buttonhole layer room to sit.

side seam.d: The seam that runs down each side of a garment, under the arm or along the hip.

slip stitch.d: A nearly invisible hand stitch for hems: a tiny catch in the main fabric, then a slide inside the fold.

spool pin.d: The post on top of the machine that holds your spool of thread.

stitch length.d: How long each stitch is, in millimeters. 2.5 mm is the everyday length for seams.

tailor's chalk.d: Flat chalk for marking fabric. It brushes off.

take-up lever.d: The arm that moves up and down above the needle. It pulls each stitch snug, and the thread must pass through it.

tension.d: How tightly the threads are held as stitches form. Balanced tension means the threads lock inside the fabric.

topstitch.d: Stitching on the right side that shows, used to hold layers flat and as decoration. Usually 1/4 in or so from an edge or seam.

trim.d: Cutting away extra seam allowance, like snipping the point off a corner so it turns out sharp.

universal needle.d: The everyday machine needle, with a slightly rounded point that works on most wovens and many knits.

woven.d: Fabric made of threads crossing over and under each other at right angles. Wovens don't stretch much, except on the bias.

wrong side.d: The back of the fabric, meant to face the inside. In Notch diagrams it's striped.

yardage.d: How much fabric a project needs, measured in yards (or meters). It depends on the fabric's width.

yoke.d: A fitted piece across the shoulders (on shirts) or hips (on skirts and jeans) that other pieces hang from.

zigzag stitch.d: A side-to-side machine stitch. Used to finish raw edges and, later, for stretchy fabrics.
